strengths: Novel and well-motivated direction: extending learning-to-learn (L2L) to zeroth-order LLM fine-tuning, with a compelling 'train once per base LLM, reuse across tasks and derivative checkpoints' framing supported by the LLM supply-chain observation.

Memory-efficient design is well justified: the per-block PertNN parameterization is motivated by the approximately block-diagonal Hessian of LLMs, and the empirical ablation (Table 4) confirms block-wise sharing beats layer-wise sharing. Overhead is minimal (62 vs 61 GB for OPT-30B; <3.4% time overhead).

Broad empirical evaluation: 4 LLMs (1B to 30B), 7 datasets, 28 task-model pairs, with convergence curves, accuracy/F1 tables, learning-rate sensitivity analysis across all models, and memory/time breakdowns in the appendix.

Useful practical analyses: normalization to decouple learned variance from effective learning rate, periodic reset during meta-training, and an honest accounting of the one-time meta-training cost (Table 8) and the gradient-truncation approximation used to make meta-training feasible.
Limitations and future work are discussed candidly, and hyperparameter grids for all baselines are provided, supporting fair comparison and reproducibility.
weaknesses: Potential train/test leakage: the ZO Fine-tuner is meta-trained on the COPA dataset and then also evaluated on COPA as a downstream task. COPA results (where ZO Fine-tuner is often the best) may be inflated; the paper does not address or ablate this concern.

The headline claims need nuance: 'outperforms in 82.1% of combinations' is measured on converged training loss; accuracy wins are only 75.0% with a modest 2.5% average improvement over MeZO, and some settings show ZO Fine-tuner losing clearly (e.g., Qwen-14B WSC 0.76 vs 0.79; OPT-30B SST-2 accuracy below several baselines). No statistical significance testing is provided despite noisy small datasets (COPA, WSC).

Theoretical support is informal and not rigorous: Theorem 1 is explicitly informal, Theorem 3 holds only in an 'ideal situation', and the appendix proof contains hand-wavy steps (e.g., exchanging expectations and invoking block-diagonality to turn a sum of conditional bounds into a joint bound) without full justification.

Internal inconsistencies undermine confidence: the appendix states a 2-layer MLP with 64 hidden units (B.3) but the runtime analysis says 32 hidden units (C.2); the text claims auxiliary-network storage under 2MB for OPT-30B, yet measured memory shows a ~1GB gap (62 vs 61 GB); the code availability URL appears truncated/missing.

The 'memory-efficient' premise is partially undercut: meta-training requires full backpropagation through the LLM (332GB for OPT-30B, Table 8), i.e., as expensive as first-order Adam training, and gradient flow through the finite-difference estimator is cut off, making the meta-objective an approximation whose bias is not analyzed.

Baselines could be stronger: several methods cited in the introduction (MeZO-SVRG, ZO-DAP) are not compared; there is no comparison to simply tuning a per-block static variance scale, which would isolate how much the learned, adaptive variance actually contributes beyond the normalization trick.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored direction: applying learning-to-learn (L2L) to zeroth-order optimization at LLM scale. The framing of 'train once per base model, reuse across tasks and derivative checkpoints' is compelling and well-motivated by the observation that most HuggingFace checkpoints are derivatives of a few base models.

The per-block variance design is well-motivated by the block-diagonal Hessian structure of LLMs and achieves extreme compactness (e.g., <2MB auxiliary networks for OPT-30B), making the L2L approach feasible where coordinate-wise designs would be prohibitive.

The evaluation is broad in scope: 4 LLMs (up to OPT-30B) × 7 datasets, comparisons against multiple recent ZO baselines (MeZO, MeZO-AdamU, LOZO, HiZOO), learning-rate sensitivity studies, ablations on normalization/periodic reset/sharing granularity, and thorough memory and runtime breakdown analyses (Tables 6-8).

The normalization trick decoupling the learned variance from the effective learning rate is a sensible and clearly explained design choice, supported by an ablation (Table 2) showing it matters substantially.
Reproducibility is reasonably supported: hyperparameter grids for all methods are reported (Table 5), meta-training costs are disclosed (Table 8), and code is stated to be released.
weaknesses: Potential task leakage / selection bias in the headline results: the ZO Fine-tuner is meta-trained on COPA, and COPA is also one of the seven evaluation datasets. The strongest gains are reported exactly on the training distribution, and 'training on a single dataset can outperform multi-dataset training' (Appendix C.5) raises the question of whether the learned optimizer overfits to COPA-like signals rather than learning a generally useful perturbation strategy. Results on COPA should be separated from the transfer claim.

The cross-model generalization claim is overreached. The finetuner is meta-trained per base model (Table 8 reports per-model meta-training), and cross-architecture transfer is never tested; the only derivative-model experiment is LLaMA-3.1-8B → LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct (same family, same size). The abstract's 'train once, reuse widely' framing is thus supported only in a narrow sense.

The theory is weak and partially mismatched with the method. Theorem 3 is explicitly in an 'ideal situation,' informal, and essentially reduces to plugging block-wise σ_j into the existing MeZO bound; the 'strictly tighter upper bound' claim is loose and not quantified. Moreover, the proof analyzes block-by-block sequential perturbation while Algorithm 1 perturbs all blocks simultaneously with a shared Σt, so the theoretical guarantee does not directly cover the actual algorithm.

Empirical gains are modest and inconsistent. The average accuracy improvement over MeZO is 2.5%, and several cells in Table 1 show the proposed method worse in loss or accuracy (e.g., Qwen-14B SST-2 loss 0.24 vs MeZO 0.21; Qwen-14B WSC accuracy 0.76 vs baselines 0.79). No statistical significance testing or seed-level variance reporting on the final Table 1 metrics is provided.

Several important methodological details are under-specified or inconsistent: the auxiliary network hidden size is stated as 64 in B.2/B.3 but 32 in C.2; the periodic-reset interval (a critical hyperparameter for meta-training) is not included in Table 5; and the one-step, myopic meta-objective with gradient cut through the finite-difference term is an approximation whose consequences are not analyzed beyond a passing remark.

Baseline coverage has gaps: MeZO-SVRG and ZO-DAP are cited as relevant improved MeZO variants but not compared; no LoRA/first-order accuracy reference points are included in the main table, making it hard to judge where ZO methods stand on the accuracy-memory Pareto frontier.

The '82.1% win rate' headline conflates training-loss wins with deployment-relevant outcomes; since the method's main selling point is downstream performance, accuracy/F1 wins (75.0%) and their magnitude deserve equal billing, and the loss-based claim is vulnerable given the optimizer is trained to minimize loss.

strengths: Novel and sensible application of learning-to-learn (L2L) to zeroth-order LLM fine-tuning; the per-block shared variance design, motivated by the approximately block-diagonal Hessian structure, makes L2L feasible at LLM scale with negligible overhead (<2MB auxiliary parameters for OPT-30B).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 4 LLMs (1B–30B) × 7 datasets (28 task-model pairs), four ZO baselines, learning-rate grid search for all methods, learning-rate sensitivity analysis, memory/time profiling, and ablations for normalization, periodic reset, and sharing granularity.

The 'train once, reuse widely' framing is well-motivated by the LLM supply-chain observation, and the demonstrated transfer from LLaMA-3.1-8B to LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct supports the practical value of the approach.

Good reproducibility: hyperparameter grids for all methods are provided (Table 5), implementation details are thorough (including the gradient cut-off approximation in meta-training), and code is released.
Clear and largely honest discussion of limitations (diagonal variance structure, meta-training overhead quantified in Table 8).
weaknesses: Theoretical contribution is weak. Theorem 3 is stated only for an 'ideal situation' and its proof contains questionable steps: the block-wise bound derivation loosely interchanges E[Σ_MB,j(θ_t,j)] with Σ_MB(θ_t), and the equality justifying summation relies on an idealized block-diagonal Hessian that holds only approximately in practice. Moreover, the proof analyzes block-by-block sequential perturbation, whereas Algorithm 1 perturbs all blocks simultaneously with distinct variances, creating a gap between theory and the actual method.

Gains over the strongest baselines are modest and inconsistently supported: the headline 2.5% accuracy improvement is over MeZO, while improvements over LOZO and HIZOO are often small, and in several cells ZO Fine-tuner loses (e.g., WSC accuracy on LLaMA-1B is 0.56 vs MeZO's 0.62 despite much lower loss; CB accuracy on LLaMA-8B). No statistical significance tests or cross-seed error bars are reported; the shaded regions in Figure 2 reflect std of smoothed loss, not run-to-run variance.

Potential evaluation contamination: the ZO Fine-tuner is meta-trained on COPA, which is also one of the seven evaluation datasets, and COPA is among the tasks where the method's advantage is most pronounced. A held-out protocol (or explicit exclusion) would strengthen the generalization claims.

The claim of reduced hyperparameter burden is undermined in practice: the method still undergoes the same learning-rate grid search as baselines, and the meta-training itself introduces additional hyperparameters (η1, η2, reset period) tuned empirically.

Several important design approximations are unablated, e.g., cutting the gradient through the finite-difference term during meta-training, and the sensitivity of the learned optimizer to the choice of meta-training dataset is only partially explored (Appendix C.5 shows single- vs multi-dataset results are comparable, but the robustness of this conclusion is unclear).

Presentation issues: redundant and inconsistent theorem numbering (Theorem 1 in the main text vs Theorems 2–3 in the appendix), grammatical errors (e.g., 'due to COPA's ... yield fast cycles'), and accuracy context is missing—reporting first-order fine-tuning reference numbers would help readers judge how much of the gap to Adam is closed.

strengths: Well-motivated extension of learning-to-learn (L2L) to zeroth-order LLM fine-tuning. The block-wise perturbation parameterization is a sensible, memory-efficient way to scale learned optimizers (e.g., <2MB auxiliary parameters for OPT-30B), grounded in known block-diagonal structure of Transformer Hessians.

Broad empirical evaluation: 4 LLMs (1B–30B) and 7 datasets (28 task-model pairs), with per-task/model learning-rate grid search for all methods, plus strong recent baselines (HIZOO, LOZO, MeZO-AdamU, MeZO).

Thorough transfer analysis beyond the headline claim: transfer to a derived checkpoint (LLaMA-3.1-8B → 8B-Instruct), transfer to a substantially different task suite (MetaMathQA with GSM8K/MATH-500 evaluation), and robustness to the choice of meta-training dataset (SQuAD, SST-2).

Useful ablations (normalization, periodic reset, block- vs. layer-wise sharing, SGD vs. Adam trajectory) and honest efficiency accounting (runtime breakdown, peak memory, meta-training cost of ~2.4x first-order fine-tuning, explicitly one-time).

Reproducibility: hyperparameter grids, L2L details (including the gradient-truncation approximation), and released finetuner checkpoints/fixed-seed scripts are provided; limitations are candidly discussed in Appendix A.1.
weaknesses: Theory–algorithm mismatch: Theorem D.5 (and the proof) analyzes a setting where perturbations are sampled block-by-block, whereas the actual algorithm perturbs all blocks simultaneously with u_t ~ N(0, Σ_t Σ_t^T). The claim that block-wise variances 'yield a tighter upper bound' is stated under an 'ideal situation' and does not directly cover the deployed method, weakening the theoretical justification for the central design.

Evidence quality on the headline claim: the 82.1% figure is for training loss; the accuracy win rate is 75.0% with an average gain of only 2.5%, often on small datasets (COPA, WSC) where differences are likely within noise. No confidence intervals, significance tests, or stated number of seeds for the accuracy numbers in Table 1; several entries show the method losing to MeZO (e.g., WSC on LLaMA-8B, HIZOO/MeZO anomalies on Qwen-14B).

The 'train once, reuse widely' claim is overstated relative to the evidence: a separate ZO Fine-tuner is meta-trained for each of the four base models (cross-architecture transfer, e.g., LLaMA→Qwen, is never tested), and derivative-model transfer is shown for only one model and two datasets.

Meta-training relies on nontrivial approximations (gradient flow cut through the finite-difference term; one-step lookahead only; empirically fixed L2L hyperparameters with reset schedules 'tuned based on the first-order trajectory behavior'), so the learned optimizer's robustness to these choices is not fully characterized.

Some presentation gaps: informal theorem statements in the main text with only the formal version deferred; loss/accuracy inconsistencies in Table 1 (e.g., very low losses with mediocre accuracy for some baselines) are not explained; Figure 1 is hard to read.

strengths: The core idea—scaling learning-to-learn to LLM-scale zeroth-order optimization via compact per-block perturbation variance networks—is sensible and well-motivated by block-diagonal Hessian structure, and the memory overhead (<2MB auxiliary networks for OPT-30B) is convincingly demonstrated (Table 9).

The experimental scope is substantial: 4 LLMs (1B–30B), 7 datasets, 28 task-model pairs, with learning-rate sensitivity studies (Figures 3–5), ablations on normalization/reset/sharing granularity (Tables 2–3), derivative-checkpoint transfer (Table 4), an out-of-distribution math task (Table 5), and meta-training dataset robustness (Table 6).

The paper is transparent about computational shortcuts (gradient cutoff through the finite-difference term in Appendix B.3), replaces MeZO-Adam with MeZO-AdamU on larger models explicitly, and provides runtime/memory breakdowns (Tables 8–10), which supports reproducibility of the evaluation protocol.
Honest limitations discussion (Appendix A.1) acknowledging the diagonal-variance restriction and non-trivial L2L training cost (~2.4x FO fine-tuning time).
weaknesses: The headline claim (82.1% of combinations) is based on final training loss, not test accuracy; training loss is a weak proxy for fine-tuning quality, and on accuracy the win rate drops to 75% with small, inconsistent gains (avg 2.5%, and sometimes worse than MeZO, e.g., WSC on LLaMA-8B and SST-2 on OPT-30B in Table 1). The significance of the contribution rests on modest improvements.

The theoretical support (Theorem 3.1 / D.5) is thin and only loosely connected to the method: it assumes an exactly block-diagonal Hessian, operates in an 'ideal situation,' proves only that some block-wise variance assignment can yield a tighter upper bound, and provides no link between the learned PertNN variances and the variance choice that provably tightens the bound. The step from 'tighter upper bound under exact block-diagonality' to 'learned variances improve convergence' is not established.

Cross-model transfer claims are ambiguous: the main text says a single finetuner trained on COPA is 'reused as is across all other tasks and models,' yet Table 10 shows separate meta-training per model and the architecture is defined per parameter block of a specific model. Whether the 1B-trained finetuner is literally applied to OPT-30B (and how blocks are matched) is unclear and central to the 'train once, reuse widely' claim.

The L2L training itself introduces hyperparameters (meta learning rates, reset schedule, trajectory optimizer) that are hand-tuned per model (Appendix C.8) and not searched in the comparison grid given to baselines, which partially undercuts the robustness narrative; the baseline grid also contains only three learning rates.

Reproducibility is undermined by a placeholder code URL ('https://github.com/.') and internal inconsistencies: hidden units reported as 64 in Appendix B.2/B.3 but 32 in Appendix C.2; the Figure 4 caption mislabels the bottom panel (Qwen-14B vs. LLaMA-8B); a stray quotation mark in the Impact Statement.

Key baselines cited as motivation (MeZO-SVRG, ZO-DAP) are not compared, and the FO upper bound in Appendix C.7 confirms a non-trivial gap remains to first-order methods, limiting the practical appeal of further improving within the MeZO regime.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: extending learning-to-learn (L2L) to zeroth-order LLM fine-tuning is a natural but underexplored direction, and the 'train once per base model, reuse across tasks/derivatives' framing is practical and well argued (e.g., the supply-chain motivation in Sec. 2 and the transfer to LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct in Table 4).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 4 LLMs (1B–30B) x 7 datasets, with consistent baselines (MeZO, MeZO-AdamU, HIZOO, LOZO), matched prompt templates and LR grid searches, plus strong ablations (normalization, periodic reset, block- vs layer-wise sharing, meta-training dataset choice, SGD vs Adam trajectories).

Memory and time overhead are carefully quantified (Tables 8-10): the learned component adds <3.5% runtime and ~1GB memory over MeZO at OPT-30B scale, and the L2L meta-training cost is reported and argued to be a one-time per-model expense.

The block-wise variance parameterization is theory-motivated via an extension of the MeZO analysis (App. D) and empirically validated against a layer-wise baseline (Table 3); the normalization trick decoupling learned variance from effective learning rate is a sensible and well-explained design choice.

Transfer is tested in genuinely out-of-distribution settings: the COPA-trained finetuner transfers to GLUE/SuperGLUE tasks, span QA, derivative checkpoints, and even a math task (MetaMathQA -> GSM8K/MATH-500, Table 5), with an ablation showing COPA is not uniquely favorable (Table 6).
Honest limitations discussion (App. A.1) covering diagonal-covariance restrictions, exploitable gradient structure, and the lack of combination with LoRA/quantization/offloading.
weaknesses: The headline 82.1% claim is based on training loss, not the downstream metric; accuracy improvements are more modest (75% of combinations, average +2.5% over MeZO), and some accuracy results are mixed or regress (e.g., LLaMA-8B WSC 0.62 vs MeZO 0.63; OPT-30B OPT results are within noise of MeZO). The paper would benefit from statistical significance testing and multiple seeds; only smoothed-loss standard deviations are shown.

One of the 7 evaluation datasets (COPA) is also the meta-training dataset, so the 28-combination evaluation is partially in-distribution; this is acknowledged but inflates the transfer percentage slightly.

The learned information content is under-analyzed. PertNN inputs (block mean/var of parameters, previous variance, last losses) are nearly constant per block, so the method may effectively reduce to a learned static per-block variance schedule rather than truly adaptive control. No analysis of the learned variance profiles or what signals PertNN actually uses is provided.

The theoretical contribution is weak: Theorem D.5 is stated only 'in ideal situation' under exact block-diagonal Hessians, and the proof largely re-derives MeZO's analysis with block-wise substitutions; the gap between the assumed and actual Hessian structure is not quantified.

Gradient flow through the finite-difference term is cut off during L2L training (App. B.3), a nontrivial approximation to the stated meta-objective; the meta-objective actually optimized differs from Eq. 5 and this is not reflected in the main method description.

Minor but concerning inconsistencies suggest insufficient polish: hidden units reported as 64 (App. B.2) vs 32 (App. C.2) for the same PertNN; the code URL in the abstract is incomplete ('https://github.com/.'); MeZO-Adam is silently replaced by MeZO-AdamU on 3 of 4 models, changing the comparison set across models.

There appear to be per-model differences in training steps (20k vs 10k) and batch sizes (16 vs 4 for OPT-30B) that make cross-model comparisons of convergence speed less controlled, and the gain of the learned optimizer over simpler alternatives (e.g., a hand-tuned static per-block variance schedule, or block-wise adaptation of HIZOO-style approaches) is not isolated.
